extracted.subtask_description: Templates and practical guidance for writing formal proofs about first-order logic statements and binary relations (reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, etc.), aimed at homework and course exercises in a discrete structures class. Emphasizes matching proof structure to the first-order logical form and gives concrete starting phrases and strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal quantifier (∀x. P)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct proof: Pick an arbitrary x, then prove P is true for that choice of x. By contradiction: Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there is some x where P is false. Then derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the proof structure to the universal quantifier: choose an arbitrary element of the domain and prove the property for that element. If using contradiction, assume existence of a counterexample and derive a contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential quantifier (∃x. P)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct proof: Do some exploring and find a choice of x where P is true. Then, write a proof explaining why P is true in that case. By contradiction: Suppose for the sake of contradiction that P is always false and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving an existential, produce an explicit witness and justify why it satisfies P; alternatively you can argue by contradiction by assuming no witness exists and deriving a contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation (¬P)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct proof: Simplify your formula by pushing the negation deeper, then apply the appropriate rule. By contradiction: Suppose for the sake of contradiction that P is true, then derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logical equivalences to move negation inward (e.g., ¬∀ ≡ ∃¬) and then apply the natural direct/existential proof templates. Proof by contradiction is often natural for negated statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction (P ∧ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct proof: Prove each of P and Q independently. By contradiction: Assume ¬(P ∧ Q) then try to derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the proof by splitting into two subgoals — show P, then show Q — or assume the negation (that at least one fails) and derive contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunction (P ∨ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct proof: Prove that ¬P → Q, or prove that ¬Q → P. By contradiction: Assume ¬P ∧ ¬Q then try to derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can prove a disjunction by producing a case that holds, or by proving an implication from the negation of the other disjunct; alternatively use contradiction by assuming both disjuncts are false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication (P → Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct proof: Assume P is true, then prove Q. By contradiction: Assume P is true and Q is false, then derive a contradiction. By contrapositive: Assume ¬Q, then prove ¬P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard approaches: direct (assume antecedent), contrapositive (assume negated consequent), or contradiction (assume antecedent and negated consequent). Pick the one that simplifies the reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional (P ↔ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove both P → Q and Q → P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split the goal into the two implications and prove each using the implication proof templates; state explicitly that both directions are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the proof to the first-order definition
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to prove that a statement is true and that statement is specified in first-order logic, look at the structure of that statement to see how to structure the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the logical form (quantifiers/connectives) as a roadmap: decide which variables to pick arbitrarily, which assumptions are antecedents to assume, and whether to aim for existence/witness construction or universal reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not restate external definitions; use them
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re proving something about an object that’s explicitly defined somewhere, you should not repeat the definition of that object in the proof. Don’t restate definitions; use them instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an object (e.g., a relation S) is defined outside the proof, expand/use the definition as needed inside the argument but avoid re-declaring the whole definition at the proof start; this keeps proofs concise and focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation proof template
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove R is an equivalence relation, prove that R is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State that you'll prove the three properties, then handle each as a mini-proof (you may split into lemmas or keep as clearly demarcated sections). If R is a concrete relation, do not repeat its definition at the top of the proof; if R is arbitrary (universally quantified), explicitly introduce it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitivity proof template
rubrics_metrics.description: To show R is transitive (∀x,y,z. (xRy ∧ yRz → xRz)): pick arbitrary x, y, z from A; assume xRy and yRz; then prove xRz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If R has a concrete definition, expand xRy and yRz according to that definition (e.g., choose witnesses m,n for an 'exists k' definition). If you only know R satisfies other properties (like cyclic), invoke those properties directly rather than re-deriving them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexivity proof template
rubrics_metrics.description: To show R is reflexive (∀x. xRx): pick an arbitrary x ∈ A and prove xRx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make any assumptions about x other than membership in A. Use the concrete definition of R if available (e.g., find a k such that x + k = x), or use known properties of R when the relation is specified by its properties rather than an explicit definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetry proof template
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove R is asymmetric (∀x,y. (xRy → ¬yRx)): pick arbitrary x and y, assume xRy, and prove yRx is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can also prove asymmetry by contradiction: assume R is not asymmetric which yields ∃x,y with xRy ∧ yRx, then derive a contradiction. Begin by explicitly stating whether you are doing a direct proof or a proof by contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving 'not symmetric' (existential witness)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove R is not symmetric, show ∃x,y. (xRy ∧ ¬yRx): produce choices of x and y such that xRy holds and yRx does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A direct approach is to define or pick specific witnesses x and y and justify both parts. You may omit variable names in very short arguments, but the key is to demonstrate existence via explicit construction and justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guideline: choose explicit witnesses for existential proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving an existential statement, give explicit choices for the variables required and justify why those choices satisfy the property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main difficulty is often coming up with the witnesses; once chosen, state them and explain why they meet the required conditions. Shortcuts (omitting names) are acceptable only when clarity is preserved.
